It is just a needle, and the needle is moving in one direction.

choices.text: Swap in the spare filter. Spend the insurance.
Throttle the intake. Less air, less ash, less time.
Let it run. Replace it when it dies.

events.title: Black Rain: Water Contamination
events.bodyText: The rain is black, and it is hitting the roof in sheets, and it sounds like someone throwing gravel. It runs off the eaves in dark streaks, and the water barrels are collecting it, and the barrels are the only water you have. The rain is radioactive. It always is. But this rain is worse than the last rain, and the barrels are full of it, and the dosimeter near the barrels is reading in numbers that are not a suggestion. You can pour it out and be thirsty, or you can boil it and hope, or you can run the purifier on overtime and burn the filter. The rain keeps coming down, black and heavy, and the barrels are filling.

choices.text: Pour the barrels out. Start over when the rain cleans.
Boil what you can. The fire is cheaper than the dose.
Run the purifier on overtime. Burn the filter.

events.title: Black Rain: Caught in the Open
events.bodyText: One of your people is still outside when the black rain starts. The radio crackles: they are two hours out, the rain came faster than the weather report, and they are sheltering under a collapsed roof with the rain pooling at their feet. The rain is black and the water is rising and the dosimeter on their belt is clicking. They can wait it out, or they can run, or you can send someone out with a tarp and a second mask. Every minute they stay in the rain, the dose climbs. Every minute someone else is out there, the dose climbs for them too. The radio is still open. The silence between transmissions is the sound of the rain on the roof.

choices.text: Tell them to stay put. The rain will pass.
Tell them to run. Get to the hatch.
Send someone out with a tarp and a second mask.

events.title: EMP Storm: Electronics Failure
events.bodyText: A flash of light on the horizon, then the radio dies mid-sentence. The lights flicker and half of them do not come back. The fusion reactor detonated in the city, the one that has been critical since the exchange, and the EMP pulse came with it, a wave of nothing that fried every unshielded circuit in the valley. The dosimeter is still working — it is mechanical, thank the old engineers. The radio is dead, the geiger counter is dead, the handheld radio is dead, and the battery charger is a brick. The bunker runs on what still works, and what still works is the generator, the purifier, and the people. Everything else needs either a faraday cage or a prayer, and the faraday cage is in the stores.

choices.text: Wrap the surviving electronics in the faraday mesh.
Go mechanical. Radios are a luxury. Breathe the quiet.
Scavenge what you can from the dead devices and rebuild.

events.title: EMP Storm: Radio Blackout
events.bodyText: The band is silent. Not static, not the distant carrier wave of the settlement broadcast, not the automated military frequency. Silence, the kind of silence that means the transmitters are gone. The EMP took them, or the storm is still in the air, or something else has happened that the radio would have told you about if the radio still worked. The bunker is deaf now. No weather, no trader calls, no distress signals, no news of the world. For the first time since the exchange, you are truly alone, and the silence is heavier than the static ever was. Someone suggests repurposing the antenna for scrap. Someone else starts writing down the frequencies they remember, just in case. The radio sits in the corner, dark, and the silence fills the room like water.

choices.text: Keep someone on the radio. The silence is information too.
Repurpose the antenna for scrap. The radio is dead.
Build a faraday cage for the surviving radios. Prepare for the next one.

events.title: Acid Snow: Roof Corrosion
events.bodyText: The snow is not white. It is grey-green, and it hisses when it touches metal. The roof of the bunker is groaning under the weight of it, and the acid in the snow is eating through the sealant, the paint, the thin layer of protection that was already thin before the exchange. The roof is the bunker's skin, and the skin is being dissolved one flake at a time. If the acid reaches the structural beams, the roof is a problem you cannot fix with a mop and a bucket. If it reaches the wiring, the lights go out. If it reaches the hatch mechanism, the hatch does not open. The snow keeps falling, grey-green, patient, and the roof is counting the hours.

choices.text: Clear the snow and reseal the roof with what you have.
Let it slide. The roof was built for worse.
Cover the roof with tarps. It buys time, not a solution.

events.title: Acid Snow: Gear Damage
events.bodyText: The acid snow has gotten into the airlock, tracked in on boots, and it is eating through the gear stored in the alcove. The gas mask straps are brittle, the rubber cracking where the acid touched. The hazmat suit has a pale spot on the chest where the material is thinning. The spare boots are dissolving at the soles. The gear that keeps people alive outside is being degraded by the weather that is outside, and the weather does not care that it is inside now. The alcove is a small room and the damage is not yet fatal, but the gear is not replaceable, and the acid is not apologetic. You can treat the gear now, or you can replace it later, and later is more expensive than now.

choices.text: Neutralize the acid with chemicals and treat the gear.
Wash everything with clean water. Waste the water, save the gear.
It is minor. The gear will hold for another season.

events.title: Bio-Fog: Spore Exposure
events.bodyText: The fog rolled in at dawn, thick and yellow-green, and it smells like a greenhouse that has been rotting for months. It is alive. The spores are in the air, and the air is in the bunker, and three people have started coughing, a wet cough that comes from deep in the chest. The medic says it is fungal, the kind that grows in the lungs and takes months to clear. The filter is catching some of it, but not all, and the fog is sitting on the valley like a blanket. You can seal the vents and let the air go stale, or you can burn what you have to kill the spores, or you can let the fog do what it does and treat the coughs as they come. The fog is patient. The spores are already inside.

choices.text: Seal the vents. Stale air is better than spore air.
Burn sulphur in the vents. Kill the spores at the source.
Treat the coughs as they come. The fog will pass.

events.title: Bio-Fog: Zero Visibility
events.bodyText: You cannot see the hatch from the periscope. The fog is that thick, a yellow-green wall that stops at the glass and goes no further. The sentry reports that the perimeter is gone, the road is gone, the landmarks are gone, and the only thing that exists is the fog and the sound of things moving in it. The scouting party is overdue, and the radio is a hiss of interference, and the fog is alive with the sound of feet and the rustle of things that do not want to be seen. You can send someone out with a rope and a flare, or you can wait for the fog to lift, or you can fire a flare into the fog and hope. The fog does not move. It sits, and the sound of things moving in it does not stop.

choices.text: Send a rope team to find the scouting party.
Wait. The fog will lift. The scouts know the way.
Fire a flare into the fog. Give them a beacon.

events.title: Blizzard: Frozen Pipes
events.bodyText: The cold is a physical thing, a weight that presses on the walls and finds the cracks. The water pipes in the bunker have frozen, and the pump is grinding against ice, and the only water that is moving is the water in the bottles. The temperature outside is minus thirty, and the temperature inside is dropping, and the heater is running on fuel that is running out. You can thaw the pipes with the last of the fuel, or you can drain the system and live on bottles, or you can let the pipes freeze and hope they do not burst. The pipes are old and the cold is new and the math is simple: water expands when it freezes, and metal does not stretch. The pipes are counting the hours.

choices.text: Thaw the pipes with the last of the fuel. Waste the heat, save the water.
Drain the system. Live on bottles until the thaw.
Let them freeze. Hope they do not burst.

events.title: Blizzard: Snow Load on the Roof
events.bodyText: The snow is drifting against the bunker, piling up on the roof, and the beams are creaking under the weight. The roof was designed for weather, but not this weather, not three metres of snow that came in two days and is still falling. The beams are groaning, a sound you can hear through the concrete, and the ceiling in the storage room has a hairline crack that was not there yesterday. If the roof fails, the bunker is a hole in the snow, and the snow is the only thing left. You can clear the roof and risk the cold, or you can brace the beams from inside, or you can trust the engineering. The beams are still groaning, and the crack is still growing, and the snow is still falling.

choices.text: Send a crew up to clear the roof. Risk the cold, save the beams.
Brace the beams from inside. Spend the wood, save the roof.
Trust the engineering. The roof was built for this.

events.title: Glass Storm: Wind-Borne Shards
events.bodyText: The wind is carrying glass, fragments of every window that shattered in the exchange, lifted from the ruins and driven at the bunker at sixty kilometres an hour. The periscope lens is already scratched, a web of fine lines that turns the outside world into a blur. The exterior equipment is being sandblasted: the antenna, the hatch mechanism, the air intake. The sound is a constant tinkling, a high-pitched rain of shards hitting metal. If the wind shifts, it will hit the solar panels. If it lasts another day, the air intake will be clogged with glass dust. You can armor the exterior, or you can wait for the wind to die, or you can send someone out to clear the intakes. The wind is not dying. The glass keeps coming.

choices.text: Armor the exterior intakes with scrap metal.
Wait for the wind to die. Close the external vents.
Send someone out to clear the intakes. Risk the glass.

events.title: Rad-Hail: Radioactive Impact
events.bodyText: The hail is the size of pebbles, and it is radioactive. Each stone hits the roof with a sharp crack, and the dosimeter near the hatch jumps with every impact. The hail is driving the fallout into the ground, into the air, into the seams of the bunker where the concrete meets the metal. The geiger counter is a steady scream, the kind of sound that gets under the skin. The hail is not just weather; it is ammunition, and the bunker is the target. If the hail breaches the hatch seal, the dose comes inside. If it cracks the periscope, the dose comes inside. If it pools in the airlock, the dose is already inside, waiting for the next person to walk through. The hail keeps coming, and the counter keeps screaming, and the bunker is taking fire from a sky that ran out of mercy.

choices.text: Seal the airlock. Nobody goes out until the hail stops.
Set up a decontamination station in the airlock.
Ride it out. The hail will pass. The dose is already here.

events.title: Ash Lightning: Fire Hazard
events.bodyText: The lightning is striking the ash dunes, and the ash is burning. The horizon is a line of orange, a low fire that feeds on the accumulated dust of three years of fallout, and the smoke is blowing toward the bunker. The fire is not close enough to threaten the walls, but the smoke is another matter: it carries the ash, the fallout, the fine particles that the filter was not designed to catch. The air intake is pulling in smoke, and the smoke is visible in the ducts, a grey haze that settles on everything. If the fire reaches the fuel dump, the plume will be worse. If the wind shifts, the fire will come closer. The lightning keeps striking, and the ash keeps burning, and the bunker is breathing smoke that is not just smoke.

choices.text: Seal the air intake. Breathe what is already inside.
Send a crew to fight the fire at the edge of the ash dunes.
Wait and filter. The fire will burn itself out.

events.title: Thermal Inversion: Stale Air
events.bodyText: The air is not moving. A thermal inversion has settled over the valley, a lid of warm air that traps the cold, the ash, the exhaust from the generators, everything, close to the ground. The bunker's air is stale, heavy with the smell of too many bodies in too little space, and the ventilation is not pulling anything fresh in because there is nothing fresh to pull. The CO2 is climbing, not enough to kill, enough to notice. People are tired, headaches, the kind of slow poisoning that comes from breathing the same air too many times. The inversion could last another day, or it could last a week. The only way to get fresh air is to open the hatch, and opening the hatch lets in the ash, the cold, the world. The air is stale, and the bunker is breathing it, and the breathing is getting harder.

choices.text: Run the CO2 scrubber. Burn the chemicals, clean the air.
Open the hatch. Let the fresh air in, ash and all.
Endure it. The inversion will lift. The headaches will pass.

events.title: Ice Storm: Hatch Mechanism Jammed
events.bodyText: The ice has sealed the outer hatch. The mechanism is frozen solid, the hinges are locked in a fist of ice, and the manual override lever is frozen in place. The bunker is sealed, which is normally a good thing, but being sealed and being unable to open are two different things. If there is a fire, if the air goes bad, if someone needs to get out, the hatch is not an option. The ice is a centimetre thick and the temperature is still dropping, and the only way to open the hatch is to heat it from the outside, which means someone has to get outside, which means getting through the hatch. The freeze is complete. The hatch is a wall now. The wall is not moving until the ice decides to let it.

choices.text: Heat the mechanism from inside. Burn the fuel, free the hatch.
Use chemicals to de-ice the hatch. Corrode the ice, not the metal.
Wait for the thaw. The ice will melt eventually.

events.title: Black Snow: Carbon Toxicity
events.bodyText: The snow is black, not from ash but from soot, the fine carbon particulate from the oil fires that have been burning since the exchange. It coats everything, a black film that gets into the lungs, the water, the food. It is not radioactive, not in the way the ash is, but it is toxic in a different way: the carbon particles are small enough to pass through the filter, small enough to get into the bloodstream, small enough to accumulate in the body like a slow poison. The bunker is black with it. Hands leave black prints, faces are smudged, the water tastes like charcoal. The snow keeps falling, black and fine, and the bunker is breathing it, and the filter is not catching it, and the dose is not the problem. The problem is the carbon, and the carbon is already inside.

choices.text: Upgrade the filter with a finer mesh. Spend the cloth, catch the carbon.
Seal the bunker. Wait for the black snow to pass.
Wash everything. Water, surfaces, hands. Fight the black with the clean.

events.title: Blood Rain: The Red Sky
events.bodyText: The rain is red. Not the red of rust, not the red of sunset, but the deep red of blood, and it is falling from a sky that is the colour of a bruise. The rain is algae, the medic says, iron oxide, dust from the desert, the medic says, but the rain is red, and it pools on the ground like something that was alive. The children are asking questions, and the adults are not answering, and the water barrels are full of red water that nobody wants to drink. The rain is not toxic, the geiger counter says, but the rain is red, and the red is the colour of everything that went wrong. The bunker is quiet, the kind of quiet that comes after a scream, and the rain keeps falling, red and patient, and nobody is looking at the sky.

choices.text: Explain it. Algae, iron oxide, science. The rain is not blood.
Let it be. Saying it is just rain does not make it less red.
Collect the rain. Red or not, water is water.

events.title: Algae Bloom: Water Source Toxicity
events.bodyText: The creek has turned green. A bloom of irradiated algae, fed by the warmth and the runoff from the old chemical plant, has covered the water source in a mat of living green that is toxic to drink and toxic to touch. The water is the bunker's backup supply, the creek that has been running clean since the exchange, and now it is running green, and the green is not clean. The algae is producing toxins that the filter cannot catch, and the fish are floating belly-up, and the smell is the smell of a swamp that has been rotting for a thousand years. You can treat the water with chemicals, or you can find another source, or you can wait for the bloom to die. The creek is green, and the bunker is thirsty, and the algae does not care about either.

choices.text: Treat the water with chemicals. Kill the algae, save the creek.
Find a new water source. The creek is lost for the season.
Wait for the bloom to die. The algae will burn itself out.

events.title: Particulate Fog: Respiratory Crisis
events.bodyText: The fog is fine, a grey mist that is not water but dust, the accumulated particulate of three years of ash and debris, suspended in the air by a temperature inversion. It gets into the lungs, and the lungs do not forgive it. The bunker's residents are coughing, a dry cough that comes from deep in the chest, and the medic is running out of the herbs that make the tea that calms the cough. The filter is catching some of it, but the filter was designed for fallout, not for micro-dust, and the micro-dust is passing through the filter like it is not there. The fog is not leaving. It is sitting in the valley, and the bunker is sitting in the fog, and the cough is spreading from person to person like a rumor.

choices.text: Brew the herbal tea. Calm the coughs, save the morale.
Seal the sleeping quarters. Keep the dust out of the lungs.
Endure the cough. The fog will lift. The lungs will heal.

events.title: The Silence: No Wind, No Birds, No Sound
events.bodyText: The wind has stopped. Not died down, not slowed, stopped. The birds are gone, the insects are gone, the distant rumble of the generators at the settlement is gone. The world is silent in a way it has never been silent before, and the silence is louder than the noise. In the bunker, people are speaking in whispers, and the whispers are too loud. The silence is not peaceful. It is the silence of a world that has forgotten how to make sound, and the memory of sound is fading. The children do not remember birds. The adults do not remember traffic. The silence is the sound of the end, and the end is not a bang, it is a quiet that goes on forever. Someone starts humming, just to hear something. The hum is the only sound in the valley.

choices.text: Play the music box. Fill the silence with something human.
Embrace the silence. It is the only peace the wasteland offers.
Fill the void. Talk, sing, read aloud. Do not let the silence win.

events.title: False Spring: The Thaw That Lies
events.bodyText: The temperature has climbed above freezing for the first time in months, and the snow is melting, and the ground is soft, and the greenhouse is warm. It feels like spring, the kind of spring that makes people want to plant seeds and open the hatch and breathe the air without a mask. But the old hands know: this is a false spring, a thaw that comes in the middle of winter and lasts long enough to trick the plants into sprouting, and then the freeze comes back and kills everything that believed the lie. The greenhouse is full of seedlings that are reaching for the sun, and the sun is warm, and the forecast is for another freeze in three days. You can plant now and risk the freeze, or you can wait and lose the heat, or you can cover the beds and hope. The thaw is warm, and the freeze is coming, and the plants do not know the difference.

choices.text: Plant now. The freeze might miss. The food is worth the risk.
Wait. Cover the beds. The right time will come.
Heat the greenhouse. Burn the fuel, keep the seedlings alive.

events.title: Silent Spring: The Season That Should Sing
events.bodyText: It is spring. The calendar says it is spring, and the sun is warm, and the snow is gone, and the ground is soft. But there are no birds, no insects, no frogs in the creek, no green shoots pushing through the soil. The spring is silent, the way the spring has been silent since the exchange, and the silence is a reminder of everything that did not come back. The old world had birdsong and the hum of bees and the sound of things growing. This world has the wind and the ash and the quiet. The greenhouse is the only green thing in the valley, and the greenhouse is inside, and the inside is not the same as the outside. The spring is silent, and the silence is the sound of the world that was lost, and the world that was lost is not coming back. Someone plants a seed anyway, just to hear the soil move.

choices.text: Plant anyway. The birds are gone, but the soil still holds.
Gather everyone. Mourn what was lost. Name the things that are gone.
Focus on what is inside. The greenhouse is the only spring we have.

events.title: Clear Sky: The Salvage Window
events.bodyText: The sky is clear, the first truly clear sky in weeks, and the dosimeter outside reads low enough to walk. The roads are visible, the ruins are visible, the world is open in a way it has not been open since the last storm. The scouts are already at the hatch, packs on, maps out, the look of people who have been waiting for a window and just saw it open. The salvage is out there: the collapsed pharmacy, the radio tower, the supply depot that the caravan trader mentioned. The window is open, but the window is not wide. A storm could roll in by evening, or the wind could shift, or the dose could climb. The sky is clear, and the clear sky is a clock, and the clock is running. Every hour in the open is salvage, and every hour of salvage is a risk. The sky is clear, and the clear sky is a question.

choices.text: Send a full salvage team. The window is open. Fill the packs.
Send a scout only. Map the routes. The salvage can wait.
Stay home. The clear sky is a lie. The dose is never low enough.

events.title: Overcast: The Grey Ceiling
events.bodyText: The sky has been grey for two weeks, a flat grey ceiling that presses down on the valley like a lid. The sun is a rumor, a memory of light that the old hands describe to the children, and the children squint at the sky and try to imagine it. The bunker is dark, and the lamps are running on batteries that are running out, and the darkness is getting into the people the way the cold gets into the concrete. Moods are low, arguments are quick, the silence between words is longer than it was. The grey is not a storm, not a threat, not a crisis. It is a weight, and the weight is the absence of light, and the absence of light is the absence of hope. Someone lights a candle, just to see a flame. The flame is the only colour in the room.

choices.text: Light the candles. Burn the wax, see the light.
Tell stories of the sun. Remind them what it looked like.
Endure the grey. The sun will come back. It always does.

events.title: Rain: The Collection Race
events.bodyText: The rain is falling, clean rain, the kind of rain that has not passed through an ash cloud and is not carrying fallout and is not black or red or green but clear, the colour of water before the exchange. The barrels are out, the tarps are stretched, every container the bunker owns is open to the sky, and the rain is filling them. This is water you do not have to filter, do not have to boil, do not have to check with the dosimeter. It is a gift, and the gift is measured in litres, and the litres are counting down. The rain will stop, and the barrels will stop filling, and the water that was free will become the water that was, and the bunker will go back to measuring cups. The rain is falling, clean and cold, and the bunker is holding its breath.

choices.text: Collect everything. Every barrel, every bottle, every drop.
Share the news on the radio. Let the settlement know the rain is clean.
Wash everything. Clothes, floors, hands. Use the rain while it lasts.

events.title: Ashfall: The Grey Tide
events.bodyText: The ash is falling again, a fine grey powder that settles on everything like a second skin. It is not a storm, not the fallout storm that sends the dosimeter screaming, but the steady ashfall that has been the background of every day since the exchange. Today it is heavier, the flakes larger, the colour darker, and the air quality is dropping. The filter is working harder, the intake is coughing, and the ash is finding its way into the seams, the cracks, the spaces between the door and the frame. The bunker is grey with it, a fine layer on every surface, and the grey is in the lungs, the food, the water. The ash is not a crisis. It is a condition, and the condition is permanent, and the permanent is harder to fight than the crisis. Someone wipes a table, and the cloth comes away grey, and the grey is the colour of the world now.

choices.text: Clean everything. Fight the grey with discipline.
Accept the grey. The ash is the world now. Wiping it away does not change it.
Seal the bunker tighter. Tape the seams, block the cracks.

events.title: The Snoring Feud
events.bodyText: Two adults in the north corridor have not spoken since the rations meeting. The argument is about the snoring. The snoring is about the bunks. The bunks are not movable. The bunkers are not un-snorable. The wall of the corridor has absorbed enough of the argument that the chalk budget is calling itself an apology.

choices.text: Sit between them at the next meal. Do not say anything. The argument ends when no one says anything.
Reassign one adult to the spare cot in the storeroom. The snoring will be the storeroom's problem now.

events.title: The Missing Keepsake
events.bodyText: The carved wooden bird that lived on the third bunk's pillow has been gone for three shifts. The child who carved it has not noticed yet. The adult whose pillow it stood against has noticed, and has started making the bunk with the blanket folded over the spot where it used to stand. Nobody has asked about it aloud, which is how everyone knows the whole corridor is thinking about it.

choices.text: Put it back. The third-bunk's pillow is where the bird was carved for.
Leave it where it is. The adult who picked it up needed it more.

events.title: The Forbidden Dial
events.bodyText: At two in the morning someone set the radio dial to 88.5 and did not log it. The shelter's frequency schedule closes that band between eleven at night and five, and the schedule is the kind of rule that exists because something happened once. The log sits blank for that hour, and the operator has left it blank on purpose, to see who comes to fill it.

choices.text: Make this a one-time exception in the binder. The dial stays at 88.5 for an hour.
Reset the dial to the official rotation. Do not name the listener.

events.title: The Pencil That Was Wrong
events.bodyText: The morning forge roster carried three names, and one of the three showed. The one who showed did the work of three, and has not said anything, but the not-saying has a shape to it, and the shift can read the shape. The roster sheet is still posted. Nobody has crossed the two names out, which is the accusation.

choices.text: Call the missing names to the council sheet. Read the pencil aloud.
Add pen marks beside the pencil marks. The names will be written tomorrow.

events.title: Whose Bunk In The Second Hour
events.bodyText: Twice this week someone has been sleeping in the second bunk of the south corridor during the second hour of second watch, and the bunk does not belong to their rotation. The person it belongs to has found it warm both times, and the warmth is the evidence, and the evidence is being discussed in low voices at the water point.

choices.text: Hand the visitor their own bunk assignation. The corridors are not for visitors.
Say nothing. The bunk has chosen its guest.

events.title: The Sermon After Quiet Hours
events.bodyText: For three nights someone has been speaking the ash cant to the children after quiet hours, in the cold room. The cant is not in the curriculum, and the curriculum is one hour a day, and the children are listening longer than an hour. The teacher has noticed the children repeating the words during lessons. The teacher has not reported it yet, and the not-yet is starting to look like a choice.

choices.text: Move the cold room door to require two signatures after quiet hours. The cant will have to wait.
Add the cant to the curriculum. The teacher's pencil will write it in.

events.title: The Walkout That Was Inherited
events.bodyText: A survivor has started saying the words walk out, to nobody in particular and to everybody at once, at meals, at the water point. The words came in with the convoy, where somebody else said them and meant them. The room goes quiet every time. The quiet is the threat's audience, and the threat is learning the room.

choices.text: Open the door. They go when they need to go. They come back when they come back.
Call the council. The pencil rolls. The threat rolls too.

events.title: Chalk Vs Chalk
events.bodyText: Two sides of the corridor are arguing about a census number, which stall it belongs to, and the argument has taken to the walls: one side writes in pencil, one side writes in chalk. The writing is polite. The two sides have stopped speaking aloud for a week, and the wall does the talking now, and the wall gets more legible every day.

choices.text: Adopt pen-only on the census board. The chalk is for letters, not numbers.
Leave the dispute for the next council. The corridor will be patient.

events.title: An Overheard Scoop
events.bodyText: The morning scoop happened in the corridor at the usual hour, and three adults watched it, and two said nothing, and one said too much: a number, a name, a comparison. The words are still in the corridor at shift change. The one who said them has not taken them back, and there is no way to take them back.

choices.text: Pull the speaker into the council sheet. Without a witness. The corridor has enough.
Open the floor at the next council. The corridor heard it; the council can too.

events.title: The Dry-Ration Loss
events.bodyText: Three tins of dry rations are gone from the back shelf, and the tally says three, and the shelf says three, and the count has not been reported yet because reporting it means counting everyone, and counting everyone means trusting no one. The shelter walks past the shelf without looking, which is the shelter's way of looking.

choices.text: Put a lock on the bulk store. The bunk that did not want lock will not say so.
Tally twice a day for a week. The pencil was made for this.

events.title: The Scoop That Went Uneven
events.bodyText: Three days running the morning scoop has come out uneven: the bowl on the left stack fuller than the bowl on the right, and the right bowl is the one the lead medic cuts from, and the difference is small, and the difference has been noticed, and the noticing is the kind that does not go back. Someone has started arriving early to watch the scoop, and the watching has been noticed too.

choices.text: Rotate who holds the scoop. The lead medic releases the spoon at dawn.
Acknowledge the double scoop. The lead is permitted extra until the schedule catches up.

events.title: The First Tin Disappears
events.bodyText: The first tin of sardines has gone from the back shelf, and the taking was deliberate: the tally knows, the shelf knows, and whoever took it knows that both can tell. It is the first tin that matters. The first tin decides whether there is a second one, and the shelter is going about its day, and the day is keeping count.

choices.text: Log the loss on the council sheet. The pencil is not for blaming. The pencil is for counting.
Share a tin on the next scoop. The imaginary first tin cannot be missed if the next tin is shared.

events.title: Feast Day Is Not A Holiday
events.bodyText: Two adults have requested a feast scoop for the second anniversary of the bunker opening. The feast scoop is not in the schedule, and the schedule is why the request could be made at all, calmly, on paper. The request sits on the council sheet now, and the council sheet is the shelter's way of holding a feast without holding one.

choices.text: Honor the feast scoop. The pencil rounds; the bowl rounds; the calendar rounds.
Defer to next quarter's review. The schedule is the schedule.

events.title: The Sick Get More
events.bodyText: The sick in the infirmary get extra, and the extra is written in the medic's pencil, and the dwellers' pencil did not get to agree. The extra is medic-grade and not negotiable at the scoop, and nobody has said it is negotiable, out loud. It is the first item on the next council sheet, which is where the saying goes.

choices.text: Confirm the medic's extra on the council sheet. The infirmary is the infirmary.
Audit the medic's extra in the next quarter. The pencil wants receipts.

events.title: A Tin With Bearings
events.bodyText: A tin was taken, and someone who did not need it saw the taking, and the sawdust block fell out of a pocket, and the block has a print on it, and the print belongs to the second bunk, and the second bunk takes the lead medic's spoon in the morning. The evidence sits in a cup on the council table, and the cup has not been discussed, and the cup is going to be discussed.

choices.text: Pull the second-bunk into the council sheet. The fingerprint is the evidence. The council sheet is the verdict.
Tally twice a day for a week. The pencil sits down. The lead does not name.

events.title: Resentment In Slow Motion
events.bodyText: The pencil wrote four kinds of resentment lines this week. The first was at the scoop. The second was at the sick list. The third was at the walking-out procession. The fourth is at the corridor clock. The resentment has not crossed 0.70 in any line. The resentment is below the threshold. The resentment is below the threshold by design.

choices.text: Pull the four pencils to one meal, alone. The resentment will name itself or it will not.
Let the resentment settle below the threshold. Below the threshold is where ration conflict is supposed to live.

events.title: The Walkout
events.bodyText: Three adults walked out at dawn. They said they would, and then they did, and the corridor door is still warm from their hands, and the shelter stands around the door without touching it. The pencil in the log does not know how to write warm. The dawn is colder than the door.

choices.text: The corridor is theirs to walk out of. The corridor is theirs to walk back into.

events.title: The Lead Pipe Went Out
events.bodyText: The lead pipe for the second bunk's circulation was pulled before dawn and left lying on the concrete, and the pulling took hands, and the hands were steady, and the shelter is doing the arithmetic of whose hands could have done it, and the arithmetic is coming out too long, which is the sabotage's second purpose.

choices.text: Pull the council sheet out. The lead pipe will be next to the pencil at the council sheet.

events.title: The Chalk Under The Doorway
events.bodyText: There is chalk under the leadership doorway. The chalk says nothing in particular: just the date of the next council meeting, underlined twice, which is not a threat, which is the shape of a threat. Forty-eight hours to the meeting. The chalk has not been picked up, and nobody is going to pick it up before the meeting.

choices.text: Acknowledge the chalk at the next council sheet. The doorway is one of the surroundings.
Step down before the council sheet. Leadership returns the chalk to its owner.

events.title: The Walkout Comes Back
events.bodyText: The same three came back at noon. They did not announce it. They walked in past the chair that sat empty by the door for the four hours they were out, and the chair was occupied again by evening, and nobody said welcome back, and nobody refused to say it, and the door has been left unlocked since, which is the shelter's speech.

choices.text: Hand them a bowl. The bowl does not ask questions. The corridor has just enough bowl.

events.title: After The Keepsake
events.bodyText: The carved bird is back on the third bunk's pillow, set the same way it stood before, and whoever returned it knew how it stood, which is the whole confession and the whole apology. The child still has not noticed. The one whose pillow it leans against has noticed, and has said nothing, and the nothing has been said kindly.

choices.text: Say nothing about it. The pillow says enough.

events.title: Before The Walkout
events.bodyText: The pencil has written the conditions on the wall by the corridor door: write when you leave, write why you leave, write when you come back. The conditions are not a law. The conditions are what the shelter could agree on with its hands shaking, and the doorway watches the pencil, and the pencil watches the doorway.

choices.text: Set the conditions in the binder. The doorway follows the binder.

events.title: Reconsidering The Walkout
events.bodyText: The walkout's threat does not need another walkout; it needs a pencil, and it got one. The threat was written down at the council table, and the writing is shorter than yesterday's threat, and shorter is the direction the shelter is trying to walk.

choices.text: Ask for a written walkout letter. The pencil will be there.

events.title: The First Testimony
events.bodyText: Following a harrowing rad-hazard shift, a survivor gathers peers in the lower workshop. Holding up a charred iron fitting and a handful of grey grit, they speak not of despair, but of purpose: whether through the memory of the Ash Witnesses, the labor of the Rebuilders, or the listening watch of the radio dial, survival must be more than waiting for filters to choke.

choices.text: Acknowledge their words. The bunker needs conviction to endure.
Urge focus on physical duties. Ideology must not distract from maintenance.

events.title: The Still Hour
events.bodyText: A quiet observance in the dormitory corner after shift change: the adherents sit together and breathe in time with the intake pulse and recite the names of former dwellers, and the names are the part the corridor stops walking past. Nerves the sedatives did not reach have started settling there, and the infirmary has noticed, and the infirmary has not objected.

choices.text: Allow the observance to continue uninterrupted.
Strictly enforce sleep regulations and extinguish remaining candles.

events.title: The Candle in the Duct
events.bodyText: A tallow stub burned in an air intake niche during the dawn vigil, and the machinist found it this morning and carried it, smoking, to the dormitory: the fat wasted, the soot in the duct, the risk written on the filter. The believers say the light was a memorial beacon for a lost shift. The machinist says the duct does not care what the light meant. Both are right, and the stub sits burned out on the table between them.

choices.text: Confiscate unauthorized fuel. Operational safety precedes ritual.
Designate an unventilated stone alcove for safe memorial lights.

events.title: The Split Reading
events.bodyText: The movement has split over a sign: the storms. One side reads the mounting storms as an order to seal the shelter against the outside forever, and has started drafting the sealing. The other reads the same storms as a mandate to send scouts out and find the enclaves still alive, and has started volunteering. Both sides cite the same text. Both sides have numbers. The shelter watches its movement divide over the sky.

choices.text: Call a joint council to reconcile their views through practical shelter priorities.
Remain neutral and let each group work out its own convictions.

events.title: The Silent Dial
events.bodyText: For two weeks the Listener kept the vigil at the radio, and the pattern repeated, and the faith had a frequency. Then the frequency flattened into an automated test tone, endless and indifferent. The Listener sits before the dial with trembling hands, and the hands are not tuning anything anymore, and the room has stopped asking whether the pattern will come back, because the asking is the wound.

choices.text: Offer personal comfort. Meaning comes from our care for each other, not the radio.
Reassign them immediately to workshop shifts to break the fixation.

events.title: The Preacher at the Pump
events.bodyText: A survivor has started speaking by the water filtration bay every day, not preaching, talking, at first. The talk is about the pumps and the soul in the same sentence, and the crowd grows every shift change, and the crowd is the part leadership has started counting. The voice has not asked for anything yet. The yet is the part leadership hears.

choices.text: Recognize their moral influence and consult them on shelter morale decisions.
Remind them that leadership is collective and orders flow through formal roster lines.

events.title: The Refusal of the Order
events.bodyText: The emergency order has met a wall: movement members refuse to scrap the memorial lathe, or to work through the remembrance day, whichever it is this morning, because the order and the day have collided. They stand with linked arms before the workshop bulkhead, and the arms are not violent, and the order is not either, and the two face each other while the corridor holds its breath on whose side it is.

choices.text: Negotiate a compromise shift schedule that preserves the memorial artifact.
Threaten ration deductions and demand immediate obedience to leadership.

events.title: The Signal in the Storm
events.bodyText: In the middle of the fallout storm, with the rad counts in the red and the shelter sealed, the adherents say they heard a distress signal from the valley, the holy valley, the one the routes avoid, and they demand a sortie now, while the signal holds. The signal log shows the storm and nothing else. The log is being shown to them, and they are hearing the signal anyway.

choices.text: Hard refusal. No scout will be sacrificed for an unverified prophecy.
Authorize an intensely shielded reconnaissance only after storm peak passes.

events.title: Work as Flight
events.bodyText: Since the partner died, the survivor has worked three double shifts in the hydroponic trench and refuses the bunk, and the hands are trembling now, and the brine tanks are open, and the walking past them is not getting steadier. The shift peers have started timing the passes, quietly, and the timing is the shelter's way of not waiting for the fall.

choices.text: Order them off the roster and assign a companion to stay with them in the dormitory.
Transition them to low-risk seated inventory tallying so they stay occupied.

events.title: The Contested Mattress
events.bodyText: The new arrival sleeps on the hallway concrete, and leadership has assigned them the bunk of the dweller who died last week, and the dead one's bunk neighbor stands at the ladder and will not move: there is a custom, twenty-four hours, and the custom is not about the bunk, and everyone in the corridor knows what it is about. The new arrival stands in the hallway with the bag, and the bag is not the problem.

choices.text: Honor the empty-bunk night. Provide extra blankets in the common room for tonight.
The living take precedence over the dead. Assign the mattress immediately.

events.title: The Dead Man's Boots
events.bodyText: The fallen scout left boots, insulated rubber, nearly new, and the expedition team wants them for the surface locker, because the boots are what boots are for, and the closest companion wants them kept in the footlocker, because the boots are also the last shape of the person who wore them. Both arguments are true. The boots sit between them, and the boots are not deciding.

choices.text: Transfer the boots to the expedition pool. Cold feet on the surface kill.
Allow the companion to keep an inscribed strap while releasing the boots for utility.

events.title: The Unfinished Promise
events.bodyText: A survivor asks for authorization to go to the radio tower on the ridge, the one the routes go around, because a fallen comrade promised to climb it and the promise is still out there, unkept. The route is the kind other routes go around. The one asking knows this. The asking is not about the route.

choices.text: Forbid the journey. We do not throw living lives after completed deaths.
Authorize the expedition only if a veteran scout accompanies them.

events.title: Highland Feral Goat Sighting
events.bodyText: Scout lookouts on the surface blast berm report a line of shaggy, thick-horned feral goats descending from the highland bluffs toward the lower scrub basin. Their winter coats are heavy with grey frost, and their hooves kick up small dust plumes along the highway embankment. The herd offers a prime, temporary hunting window before wolves push them further south.

choices.text: Dispatch an expedition team to set heavy snare lines along the defile.
Let the herd pass undisturbed to avoid drawing predator attention.

events.title: Estuary Mirror Carp Surge
events.bodyText: The river water churns with heavy silver-scaled mirror carp pushing upriver against the spring thaw current. Their armored backs break the brown foam as they congregate in shallow gravel shoals. For the next several weeks, basket nets and weir traps along the riverbank can yield substantial fresh protein.

choices.text: Construct willow weir baskets to harvest spawning carp in bulk.
Assay the river current for dissolved isotope runoff before harvesting.

events.title: Ghost Moth Swarm Front
events.bodyText: A warm humid wind carries a pale, undulating cloud of ghost moths inland across the lowlands. Thousands of fluttering wings beat against outer intake grates, leaving sticky white web fibers and powdery scales that quickly choke air filters and threaten outdoor cultivation beds.

choices.text: Batton intake cowls and burn sulfur torches around exterior vents.
Send sweepers with scrapers to harvest silk pupae clusters for roasting.

events.title: Ash Boar Sounder Crossing
events.bodyText: A dozen massive, bristled ash boars churn the river mudbank, rooting deep into acorn scrub and tearing apart rotting railway ties. Their heavy tusks gouge the soil, exposing buried cables and pre-war drainage pipes. A disciplined hunting party could harvest heavy pork rations, but a cornered sounder will crush unarmored scouts.

choices.text: Stalk the sounder at the creek crossing with heavy caliber rifles.
Hold position and allow the sounder to disperse into the oak hills.

events.title: Iron Crow Railway Flyway
events.bodyText: Hundreds of metallic-sheened crows descend onto the rusted steel transmission towers along the railway cut. Their rhythmic cawing echoes across the valley as they roost for the night before continuing south. Flocks of this size strip dead wood of grubs and clean the tracks of carrion, leaving clear signs of predator activity down the line.

choices.text: Analyze the crows' flight vectors to pinpoint fresh carrion or predator locations.

events.title: Lowland Cotton Hare Population Boom
events.bodyText: Following a mild thaw, cotton hares have multiplied across the southern floodplains. Their white summer coats flash across the heather as hundreds of young feed on succulent scrub shoots. Snares set along hedgerows can double their typical catch over the next week.

choices.text: Double the snare line density across the floodplain brush.

events.title: Faction Gunfire Blocks Migration Corridor
events.bodyText: Mortar fire and fortified barricades at the highway junction have severed the traditional descent route for feral goat herds. Cut off from winter foraging, the starving animals are forced into dense predator-rich canyon defiles, causing herd numbers to plummet while ravenous wolf packs circle closer to perimeter watchposts.

choices.text: Mark an unmined defile to guide remnant herds away from gunfire.
Double perimeter sentries against starving wolf packs stalking the corridor.

events.title: Toxic Slag Runoff Taints River Fish
events.bodyText: A ruptured tailings dam upstream has discharged acidic heavy-isotope slurry into the river. Dead mirror carp float belly-up along the reeds, their gills stained bright copper. Any fish harvested without thorough decontamination will cause severe radiation sickness.

choices.text: Post biohazard flags and suspend all river netting until currents flush clean.

events.title: Moth Blight Decimates Surface Forage
events.bodyText: Caterpillar swarms from the recent moth bloom have stripped wild berry canes, willow saplings, and wild grain patches down to bare wood. With natural vegetation devastated, ground rodents are invading agricultural silos and shelter pantries searching for sustenance.

choices.text: Seal all grain barrels with bitumen pitch and set poison traps in corridors.

events.title: Acidic Ash Storm Grounds Passage Flock
events.bodyText: A violent fallout squall caught a flock of iron crows mid-flight, coating their feathers in corrosive gypsum sludge and forcing hundreds of grounded birds into the shelter's surface intake berm. Their distressed alarm calls are attracting scavenging rad dogs to the gate.

choices.text: Clear the intake area and drive off lurking wild dogs with warning shots.

events.title: Scavenger Kettle Circling Downwind
events.bodyText: A spiral of crows and ash gulls is circling low over an overgrown culvert two kilometers down the rail line. Such kettles indicate a fresh carcass or an abandoned scavenger haul before ground predators have claimed it.

choices.text: Dispatch a rapid scout pair to salvage the carcass before wolves arrive.

events.title: Fresh Boar Wallower Discovered
events.bodyText: Scouts have identified an active boar wallow in the creek muds, rich with musky scent and fresh hoof impressions. Setting a staked deadfall trap before dusk guarantees a heavy game catch when the sounder returns to bathe.

choices.text: Construct heavy timber deadfalls over the wallow crossing.

events.title: Abandoned Slag Hornet Comb
events.bodyText: Winter frost has killed off an exterior slag hornet colony in the quarry overhang. The papery carton hangs silent and cold, packed with uncontaminated comb wax and medicinal propolis resin ready for safe harvesting.

choices.text: Cut down the winter comb for medical and sealing supplies.

events.title: Bio-Remediation Fungal Mat Assay
events.bodyText: In a damp concrete overflow drainage ditch, an unusual black-and-gold fungal mat has colonized mineral sludge. Preliminary dosimeter sweeps show the living mycelium is actively absorbing and concentrating radioactive isotopes from runoff water, leaving the outflow significantly cleaner.

choices.text: Collect spore cultures to seed shelter wastewater filtration channels.
